nominal

/NOM-uh-nul/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Nominal means existing in name only, not in reality; it can also describe a token amount far below the real value, as in a nominal fee.

The museum charges a nominal admission fee of fifty cents, a symbolic price meant only to remind visitors that the collection has worth.

Example

Although the aging king remained the nominal head of state, every real decision was made by the council of ministers. His role had shrunk to waving from balconies and signing papers the council had already approved.

The king holds the title in name only while others hold the actual power, which is exactly what nominal means when applied to a role or position.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

token: Token describes something offered as a gesture rather than for real effect: a token effort, a token apology. Nominal makes a claim about names and numbers: a nominal title or nominal price exists in name only, with the reality far smaller than the label suggests.

symbolic: Symbolic means standing for something rather than truly being it: a symbolic handshake, a symbolic first pitch. Nominal is narrower and cooler. It says a name, title, or price is technically there but hollow in practice, the way a nominal ruler reigns while a council governs.

so-called: So-called flags a name the writer doubts or mocks: the so-called expert who fixed nothing. Nominal reports a mismatch neutrally, saying the title or amount is genuine on paper yet empty in practice. So-called sneers at the label, while nominal simply measures the gap between name and reality.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

actual: existing in fact, not just in name

genuine: real and truly what it is said to be

Where it sits · how little real payment is asked

modest → nominal → free

modest vs. nominal: A modest fee is smaller than average but still a real price, while a nominal fee is a mere token far below what something is actually worth.

free vs. nominal: A nominal charge asks for a token payment, but something offered free asks for nothing at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — nomin: from Latin nomen, name

Suffix — -al: adjective-forming ending, relating to

Put it together: Nominal joins the root nomin-, from Latin nomen, 'name,' with the adjective suffix -al, 'relating to.' Something nominal exists 'in name': a leader who rules in name only, or a fee that is a price in name rather than a real one. The same root appears in nominate, 'to put someone's name forward.'

Use the root in a new word: nominee: The academy announced each nominee for the award by reading the names aloud, and nominee itself carries the same Latin root, nomen, that gives nominal its meaning of 'in name.'

Root Check

Word Choice

formal

Nominal has two closely related uses: a nominal leader holds a title in name only, and a nominal fee is a token amount far below real value, as in 'a nominal fee of one dollar.' Trivial, also taught in this unit, describes something unimportant in a different way: it is about the significance of a matter or issue, not about a title or a token amount. Nominal is not simply a fancy word for small; it always signals that the name or price does not match the reality.
